title: Why Translations Differ
subtitle: Word for word, thought for thought, and paraphrase. What each philosophy protects, and how to choose without fear.
triageNote: No article of the faith hangs on whether your Bible says propitiation or sacrifice of atonement. The major translations in every philosophy were made by believing scholars from the same Hebrew and Greek. This is a third-order question, the kind a healthy congregation contains without strain, with an ESV in one pew, an NIV in the next, and a well-worn King James by the radiator. It is on this page because the differences confuse people into distrust. And the cure for that distrust is twenty minutes of understanding what translators actually do.
question: Hold two Bibles side by side at Psalm 23 or Romans 3 and the wording differs, sometimes slightly, sometimes startlingly. Why. A small part of the answer is textual, treated on the manuscripts page of this set. The large part is translational philosophy. Hebrew and Greek are not English. Every sentence forces choices between keeping the form of the original, its word order, its idioms, its ambiguities, and conveying the sense of the original in natural English. Formal equivalence leans toward the form: the NASB, ESV, and KJV. Functional equivalence, also called dynamic, leans toward the sense: the NIV moderately, the NLT thoroughly. Paraphrase sits past the far end: The Message renders Scripture in contemporary idiom with maximal freedom. Which philosophy best serves the reader, and which Bible should you actually use, is the question. The three schools answer it with conviction.
whyItMatters:
Because the differences, met unprepared, read like contradiction. A new believer comparing Amos 4:6 finds cleanness of teeth in one Bible and empty stomachs in another and wonders which translator was lying. In fact both rendered the same Hebrew idiom for famine, one keeping the image, one cashing it out. Multiply that by ten thousand verses and you have either a reader educated into confidence or a reader frightened into thinking the Bible is soft clay. The difference is somebody explaining the craft.

Because translation is the church's oldest technology of mission. The apostles themselves worked from a translation, quoting the Greek Septuagint more often than the Hebrew. Jerome gave Latin Christendom its Vulgate around 405. Tyndale was strangled and burned in 1536 for putting the Greek into plowboy English. Ninety percent of his phrasing lives on in the King James of 1611, whose cadences carried English-speaking faith for three centuries. Eugene Nida's mid-twentieth-century theory of dynamic equivalence re-armed the Bible societies and helped put Scripture into thousands of languages. The argument on this page is not pedantry. It is the working doctrine of how the word crosses borders, including the border between the ancient world and your kitchen.

And because the practical question, which Bible should I read, deserves a straight answer rather than a tribal one. Readers have been told the literal Bibles are the holy ones, or that the readable Bibles are the honest ones, by people selling each. The truth is friendlier and more useful. The philosophies protect different things, every translation pays costs, and a reader who knows what each is protecting can choose wisely, and choose more than one.

positions.name: Formal equivalence: essentially literal
positions.inOneLine: Translate the words and structure of the original as far as English allows, transparent to what the text actually says. Trust the reader and teacher with the interpretive work the original leaves open.
positions.bestCase:
My principle is restraint, and it comes from what I believe this book is. If Scripture is God-breathed down to its words, then a translator's calling is to carry those words across, not to improve them, smooth them, or decide for you what they must have meant. Every translation interprets, I grant the slogan. But there is a world of difference between interpreting as little as the languages permit and interpreting as much as the reader will tolerate. I want the reader of English standing as close to the Hebrew and Greek as English can put him, seeing what is there, including what is strange there. The strangeness is data. Leland Ryken's way of saying it is that the translator is a steward of someone else's words, and stewardship is not authorship.

Let me show you what restraint protects. It protects metaphors, the live tissue of Scripture. When Israel's repentance fails, Hosea says Ephraim is a cake not turned. When famine comes, Amos says God gave cleanness of teeth. When the psalmist is sustained, his head is anointed with oil. Functional translations, fearing your confusion, will often hand you the point, halfway committed, hunger, honored. The point is not the same as the picture, because pictures do things points cannot. It protects interlocking vocabulary. Paul builds arguments where flesh in Romans 8 answers flesh in Romans 7. A translation that renders the word three different ways for smoothness has quietly dismantled the argument before your eyes ever reach it. It protects theological precision. Propitiation in Romans 3:25 is a hard old word. The committee that keeps it is refusing to settle, on your behalf and without telling you, a live debate about whether the cross turns away wrath or only covers sin. And it protects ambiguity itself. Where the original can be read two ways, I am honor-bound to leave you two ways if I can. The ambiguity is in the text God gave. Resolving it is the work of teachers, commentaries, and the church, in the open, with arguments you can weigh, not the silent privilege of a translator you will never meet.

The cost, I freely own, is that my translations are harder. They keep Hebrew idioms that make you slow down, sentences with Paul's own tangles, words you must grow into. I am unrepentant about that, within reason. Scripture is not a product to be made frictionless. It is a text to be lived with for sixty years. The qualities that make a text slightly harder at first reading, concreteness, consistency, density, are the very qualities that reward the five-hundredth reading. The Bible was given to be studied, memorized, preached from, and argued over. For all of that you need to know what it says, before anyone, including me, tells you what it means.
advocates: Leland Ryken (The Word of God in English, 2002)
John MacArthur and much of the expository-preaching movement

positions.name: Functional equivalence: thought for thought
positions.inOneLine: Translate so that today's reader receives, as nearly as possible, the meaning the original reader received. Faithfulness is measured at the point of understanding, not at the point of word-matching.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with what translation is for. The Bible was not written in a sacred code. It was written in the street Greek of the first century, the koine, language so ordinary that scholars once thought it a special Holy Ghost dialect. Then the papyri, shopping lists and family letters dug from Egyptian sand, proved it was the tongue of the marketplace. The New Testament met its first readers with no foreign accent. A translation faithful to that fact must meet you the same way. Eugene Nida, whose work from the 1947 Bible-translating handbook through Toward a Science of Translating in 1964 reshaped the entire field, gave the principle its name: dynamic equivalence, the closest natural equivalent of the source-language message. Natural is not a compromise word. It is the fidelity word. If the original was clear and the translation is murky, the translation has failed at the exact point where the original succeeded, however many word-matches it can show for the wreckage.

Because here is the uncomfortable truth my formal friends keep underselling. Word-for-word transfer between unrelated languages is not conservative. It is distortion with a pious face. Languages do not line up. Hebrew has no word for brain and speaks of kidneys and bowels where we say heart and conscience. Render the forms and you have produced nonsense the original never contained. The Greek genitive can mean a dozen relationships, and the love of God leaves an English reader guessing where the Greek reader was not. Idioms are the obvious case, cleanness of teeth is famine, a cake not turned is a half-baked man. But the deep case is structure. Paul's sentence in Ephesians 1:3-14 runs over two hundred Greek words, and reproducing it as one English sentence does not honor Paul, it buries him, because Greek syntax carries a long sentence the way English simply cannot. When the NIV breaks it into readable sentences, nothing is being taken from you. Meaning is being delivered, which was the assignment.

And before anyone tells you which side the Bible itself is on, open it and watch its authors translate. The New Testament writers quote the Old hundreds of times, mostly from the Greek Septuagint, freely, adaptively, by sense, with the meaning preserved and the wording bent to the audience. When Nehemiah 8 describes the first Bible-reading service after the exile, the Levites read from the Law, clearly, and gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading. Gave the sense. That is the oldest job description in translation, and it is mine. Mark, writing for Romans, translates Aramaic on the spot, Talitha cumi, which means, little girl, arise. Paul tells the Corinthians he would rather speak five intelligible words than ten thousand in a tongue. Intelligibility is not the marketing department's value. It is the apostles', and a Bible the plowboy cannot understand has not yet done what Tyndale died to do.
advocates: Gordon Fee and Mark Strauss (How to Choose a Translation for All Its Worth, 2007)
D. A. Carson (a functional priority, argued with cautions)

positions.name: Paraphrase: the text in living idiom
positions.inOneLine: Render Scripture with full freedom into the rhythms of contemporary speech. The aim is not to replace study Bibles but to ambush readers whose ears have gone dead to the familiar words.
positions.bestCase:
Let me tell you why I did it, because the why is the whole defense. I was a pastor for nearly thirty years before I was a translator, and I watched the same thing happen in study after study. I would put Galatians, Paul at his most volcanic, in front of ordinary believing people, and their eyes would glaze. Not because the words were too hard. Because they were too familiar. They had heard Bible language their whole lives, and it had become wallpaper, holy, expected, and inert. The most dangerous thing that can happen to Scripture in a churched culture is not mistranslation. It is inoculation, words so well known they can no longer bite. So I began doing for my congregation what I had been trained to do at the desk. I worked straight from the Greek with its dirt and energy intact, writing what came out in the American language people actually argue, shop, and pray in. That work, begun in a church basement, became The Message, finished in 2002 after twelve years.

Understand what a paraphrase is for, and what it is not for. I never intended it as a study Bible, and I said so plainly. When people asked if it should replace their NIV or ESV, I told them no, and I did not use The Message from the pulpit myself. A paraphrase is a reading Bible. It is for the woman who has read Psalm 23 eight hundred times and cannot hear it anymore, who needs God, my shepherd, I do not need a thing, to crack the varnish so the psalm can reach her again. It is for the man who thinks the Bible is a religious artifact, who will never crack Leviticus, but who will read narrative prose that sounds like a human being talking, and discover that the prodigal's father runs. J. B. Phillips, whose 1958 New Testament in Modern English did this work for an earlier generation, made the case in one sentence. His young Londoners, bombed and skeptical, found the Authorized Version unreadable, and when he turned the epistles into their English, the letters, he said, came off the page like live wires. Translation for the bored and the outside is its own calling, with its own fidelity, fidelity to impact, to the jolt the original delivered before it was famous.

The costs of my freedom are real, and I will name them rather than wait for my critics. I interpret, heavily, on nearly every page. Where the text is ambiguous I chose, and where the idiom needed an American body I gave it one. Anyone checking my Sermon on the Mount against the Greek will find Peterson all over it. That is why this work must live alongside the committee translations, under them, corrected by them, never instead of them. But I will not concede that the enterprise is irreverent. The precedent is the incarnation itself, and the precedent is also the Bible's own. The Septuagint paraphrases freely in places, and the Aramaic targums that Jesus' own synagogues used were interpretive renderings, expansive, vivid, and aimed at the listening ear. God has always been willing to be heard in the accents of the street. The Word became flesh and moved into the neighborhood, I wrote, and I stand by the verse and the method in the same breath.
advocates: J. B. Phillips (The New Testament in Modern English, 1958)
Kenneth Taylor (The Living Bible, 1971, written for his children at the breakfast table)

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Functional equivalence, claimed warmly by paraphrase
biblicalEvidence.summary: They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading. The post-exilic assembly likely needed the Hebrew rendered and explained in Aramaic, making this the Bible's first portrait of translation ministry, defined by delivered understanding.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any version of formalism that treats reader understanding as someone else's department.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Formal equivalence answers that the verse describes two acts, reading the text and giving the sense. The second is the teacher's office, not the translator's, which is precisely the division of labor formalism defends. The Levites explained an exact text. They did not hand the people a pre-explained one. Functional translators reply that for a people who no longer spoke the original language, the giving of the sense was the translation, and the verse blesses exactly that.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Unless you utter with your tongue speech that is intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? You will be speaking into the air. Paul's argument against uninterpreted tongues enthrones intelligibility as a governing value of speech in the church.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for translations whose English is so shaped by the donor languages that it communicates mainly to the initiated, the very in-group speech Paul is correcting.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Formal equivalence notes the context is ecstatic speech, not translation method, and warns against stretching it. Its own translations are intelligible English, merely demanding English. And Paul never equates intelligible with effortless, since Peter himself says Paul's letters contain things hard to understand. The paraphraser takes the verse the furthest: speaking into the air is what the church does every time it answers a living question in antique idiom.

biblicalEvidence.passage: The New Testament's use of the Septuagint, for example Matthew 1:23 citing Isaiah 7:14
biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Functional equivalence, with comfort for paraphrase
biblicalEvidence.summary: The apostles overwhelmingly quote the Old Testament from the Greek translation, not the Hebrew, and treat the translation as the word of God, it is written. Matthew's gospel rests a fulfillment citation on the Septuagint's rendering of Isaiah's term as virgin. Inspired authors used, trusted, and built on a translation.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any sacred-original purism that implies translations are second-class Scripture, and hard for slogans on all sides, since the Septuagint is by turns literal, free, and interpretive.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Formal equivalence agrees translations can bear the full authority of the word, that is common ground. It observes that apostolic citation practice, under inspiration, is a unique case that licenses no one's method today. Functional equivalence draws the broader, fair conclusion: the apostles' working Bible was a translation made for Greek-speaking Jews in their own tongue, which is the functional project exactly. The paraphraser adds that the targums sat beside it, freer still, in the synagogues of Galilee.

biblicalEvidence.passage: Amos 4:6 and the problem of idiom
biblicalEvidence.summary: I gave you cleanness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places. The KJV and ESV keep the grim idiom, teeth clean because there is nothing to chew. The NIV gives empty stomachs. One Hebrew line, and the whole debate in miniature: keep the picture or deliver the point.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for both sides at once, which is its value. The formal reader can miss the meaning, the functional reader has lost the irony, God's terrible gift list, I gave you, framed as blessing.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Formal equivalence argues the image is recoverable with a moment's thought or a footnote. A Bible full of cashed-out idioms becomes a Bible with no idioms, flattened of the very concreteness Hebrew poetry lives by. Functional equivalence answers that a reader who misses famine has not read the verse at all. The second clause, lack of bread, shows the Hebrew explaining its own idiom, the original doing in-line what the NIV does. Both readings are honest. That is the lesson.

biblicalEvidence.passage: Romans 3:25 and the vocabulary of atonement
biblicalEvidence.summary: God put Christ forward as a hilasterion. The ESV and NASB render propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away wrath. The NIV gives sacrifice of atonement with a footnote. The NEB once offered means of expiating sin. The choice among English words is a choice among atonement theologies, made for you by a committee.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for functional equivalence, because here the natural-English instinct, replacing a technical term with an accessible phrase, demonstrably narrows or blurs a debated meaning.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Functional translators answer candidly that propitiation is not English the reader possesses. An unknown word communicates nothing at all, which is its own infidelity, and the footnote carries the scholarship. Formal equivalence replies that hard words can be taught, that pastors exist for exactly this, and that the reader robbed of the word is robbed of the debate. The paraphraser, instructively, goes simplest of all. The Message gives a sacrifice of mercy, and openly relies on the other translations to hold the technical ground.

biblicalEvidence.summary: You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it. The canon-edges of both testaments carry warnings against adding and subtracting, and formal translators hear in them a charter of minimal interference.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for paraphrase, whose method adds and recasts on principle, and a standing conscience-check for every translator of any school.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Functional and paraphrasing translators answer that the warnings concern tampering with the substance of God's commands and the prophecy's content, not the mechanics of rendering languages. Otherwise all translation stands condemned, including the formal kind, which also adds words to make English grammar. And the Septuagint quoted by apostles condemns itself. Formal equivalence concedes the exegesis and keeps the application as a posture. The verses may not forbid free translation, but they describe the fear and trembling proper to anyone who touches these words for a living.

weighing:
My judgment, and on this page I can be the most practical, because the tentative answer is also the usable one.

The debate is real but the war is mostly marketing. The serious translations across all three philosophies were made from the same critical texts by scholars of deep faith and deeper philology. The formal Bibles interpret more than their slogans admit. Every translation is thought for thought the moment Hebrew kidneys become English hearts. And the functional Bibles are more disciplined than their critics allow, tethered line by line to the originals. Brunn's One Bible, Many Versions demonstrated this with columns of evidence. The literal versions translate freely all over the place, and the free versions translate literally all over the place, because the languages, not the philosophies, dictate most of the choices. Once you see that, you stop asking which Bible is the real one and start asking which tool fits which task. The fear goes out of the question.

So, asked plainly which to use, here is what I tell my own congregation. Anchor your study in an essentially literal translation, ESV, NASB, CSB, or the NKJV if your ears were raised on the old cadences. When you are building doctrine or tracing Paul's argument you want maximum transparency to what stands written, ambiguities and hard words included. Read at length, whole books at a sitting, in a good functional translation, NIV or NLT. Scripture is mostly story and letter and song, and it was meant to be read the way those are read, in long swallows, with understanding. And once in a while, when the familiar words have gone to wallpaper, let The Message or Phillips ambush you, on the porch, not in the pulpit. The translation that does you the most good is the one you will actually read. The reader with two open Bibles side by side has, without paying tuition, begun to see the original through the gap between them.

One verdict I will state without hedging. The existence of many translations is not the Bible's weakness but its glory. Islam holds that the Quran is properly itself only in Arabic. Christianity was born quoting its Scriptures in translation and has never met a language it would not enter. The variety on your shelf is what a Pentecost faith looks like in print.
charitableDisagreement:
Each school is guarding a treasure, and the guards need each other. The formal translator guards the text's own words against the arrogance of improvers, and every generation produces improvers. The functional translator guards the reader, and the plowboy Tyndale died for is owed a Bible he can actually understand, not a monument he can only admire. The paraphraser guards the jolt, the original scandal and speed of the word, against the deadening of familiarity, which is a real enemy the other two methods cannot reach. A church that had only formal Bibles would slowly become a church of scribes. Only functional ones, a church that never knew what it was simplifying. Only paraphrases, a church adrift from the text within a generation. The ecosystem is the safeguard.

Is any of this a hill to die on. One thing on this page is. The principle, sealed with Tyndale's blood and vindicated at Pentecost, that the word of God belongs in the language of the people. Everything else, your version preference, your church's pew Bible, your suspicion of the one your neighbor underlines, is a matter for liberty and charity. Do not let anyone make a translation into a tribal flag, and do not carry one yourself. The man with the King James and the woman with the NLT are reading the same gospel. And the Lord they meet in it did his own teaching in Aramaic, was preached in Greek, and reached you in English without losing a single sheep along the way.

relatedDebates.note: The other reason translations differ. Where the KJV reads verses that modern versions footnote, the difference is usually textual, the Textus Receptus against the critical text, not translational. The manuscripts page in this set sorts those differences. It counts the variants honestly.

The sharpest recent version of this debate: when the Greek says brothers and means the whole congregation, is brothers and sisters a clarification or a concession. The TNIV controversy of 2002 to 2005 and the 2011 NIV carried this argument through the churches. Carson's book on the inclusive-language debate remains the calmest guide.

relatedDebates.topic: The King James and its legacy
relatedDebates.note: The 1611 version is both a translation and a cultural monument. Arguments about it are usually about both at once. Its textual base, its unmatched cadences, and the King-James-only movement that grew up in the twentieth century each deserve separate, patient treatment.
